rationale: The literature consistently supports early-onset nystagmus, hypotonia, and progression to spasticity/spastic quadriparesis as core phenotypic hallmarks present in nearly all infantile-onset NKX6-2 patients (>85% to 100% across reported series, including 10/10 individuals in Baldi et al. and consistent findings across cohorts summarized by Chelban et al.). However, the secondary claim that developmental regression occurs in <35% of the global cohort is conflicted by evidence: Baldi et al. identified developmental regression in 3 of 6 families (50%) and highlighted it as an under-recognized core feature rather than a rare secondary complication, while additional reports (such as Bereshneh et al.) also document motor regression in their cases. Seizure frequencies vary across reports (e.g., observed in 2 of 6 families in Baldi et al., and occurring with or without overt hypomyelination in Chelban et al.), making a fixed global pooled estimate of <35% for both regression and seizures uncertain and contested.

evidence.text: Baldi et al. identified homozygous NKX6-2 pathogenic variants in 10 patients from 6 unrelated families. All 10 shared psychomotor delay, spastic quadriparesis, nystagmus, and hypotonia (10/10, 100%). Seizures were present in 2 of 6 families (33.3%), whereas developmental regression was documented in 3 of 6 families (50%), leading authors to emphasize clinical regression as an underestimated feature.

source.title: Expanding the clinical and genetic spectra of NKX6‐2‐related disorder
source.quote: Our patients share a primary diagnosis of psychomotor delay, and they show spastic quadriparesis, nystagmus and hypotonia. Seizures and dysmorphic features (observed in 2 families each) represent an addition to the phenotype, while developmental regression (observed in 3 families) appears to be a notable and previously underestimated clinical feature.

numbers.metric: spastic quadriparesis, nystagmus, and hypotonia penetrance in cohort

evidence.text: Chelban et al. evaluated 11 new cases from 8 families alongside previously published cases (totaling >36 subjects), concluding that NKX6-2 disorder exhibits a broad spectrum from severe neonatal onset to milder childhood onset. The authors recommend testing for NKX6-2 in patients presenting with autosomal recessive, very early onset nystagmus, cerebellar ataxia, and hypotonia progressing to spasticity, while demonstrating that epilepsy can occur even in the absence of overt hypomyelination.

source.title: Genetic and phenotypic characterization of NKX6‐2‐related spastic ataxia and hypomyelination
source.quote: NKX6-2 mutations should be considered in patients with autosomal recessive, very early onset of nystagmus, cerebellar ataxia with hypotonia that rapidly progresses to spasticity, particularly when associated with neuroimaging signs of hypomyelination.

evidence.text: Bereshneh et al. described two affected siblings homozygous for NKX6-2 c.501C>G who presented with global developmental delay, motor regression, hypotonia, spasticity, contractures, clonus, and nystagmus, adding to the growing recognition that regression occurs prominently in affected kindreds.

source.title: Expanding the clinical and neuroimaging features of NKX6-2-related hereditary spastic ataxia type 8
source.quote: In this study, we performed Whole Exome Sequencing and identified a novel missense variant, c.501C > G; p.(Phe167Leu), in two affected siblings with main manifestations of global developmental delay, motor regression, hypotonia, clonus in lower limbs and muscle bulk atrophy especially in the upper limbs, spasticity and contracture, scoliosis, hip dislocation, oculomotor apraxia, horizontal and vertical nystagmus.

numbers.metric: affected siblings presenting with motor regression and nystagmus

conflicts: Developmental regression frequency: The hypothesis posits that developmental regression occurs in fewer than 35% of cases; however, Baldi et al. identified it in 50% (3 of 6) of families and argued that regression is an under-recognized hallmark rather than an infrequent secondary feature, reinforced by case reports demonstrating motor regression in siblings.

Epileptic vs non-epileptic phenotypic spectrum: Chelban et al. demonstrated that epilepsy and hypomyelination dissociate in some families (e.g. epilepsy without overt hypomyelination, or diffuse hypomyelination without seizures), challenging rigid lower-bound prevalence thresholds for seizure occurrence across the wider phenotypic spectrum.

new_directions.question_text: What is the exact individual-level (rather than family-level) penetrance of developmental regression across all published biallelic NKX6-2 individuals?
new_directions.rationale: Clarifying whether regression is present in a strict minority (<35%) or a majority of severe infantile cases will define whether its presence or absence has diagnostic utility in separating NKX6-2 from classical Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease or epileptic encephalopathies.

new_directions.question_text: Do truncating/null variants in NKX6-2 confer higher risks of seizures and rapid regression compared to homeodomain missense variants?
new_directions.rationale: Initial studies found limited genotype-phenotype correlations in small cohorts, but expanded series stratifying by functional variant impact could explain the divergence in seizure and regression rates.
